_comment: 🔮️ Oracle contribution of the 🏃️test-runner module. Nothing third party implements this repository's scope→argv mapping, so the planning capabilities rest on frozen specification vectors; the transcript parsers rest on a second, independently written parser plus those vectors.

oracles.rationale: The six runner report dialects are emitted by the runners themselves, and no single published library parses go test -json, the vitest JSON reporter, pytest's terminal report, libtest, cargo-nextest, the dotnet console logger and rspec --format json into one common model — a library per dialect would be six oracles for one capability and four of the six have none at all. The reference is therefore a second parser written independently against the same recorded transcripts (the 🟦️.ts adapter), together with those transcripts as frozen specification vectors. vitest is a root dependency of this repository and was considered as a real oracle: it can produce the reporter document but cannot consume one, so it is evidence for the fixture's shape, not for the parse. Registered as a cross-semio-implementation reference rather than as a qualifying third-party oracle, which is exactly what it is: a second parser written inside this repository, deliberately sharing no code with the subject.

noOracleDecisions.rationale: Which bundle manifest selects which runner, and which argv a repo:// scope becomes, is this repository's own vocabulary — the bundle table, the entity-URI grammar and the narrowing order are defined nowhere outside semio, so no third-party library, CLI or standards tool can be a reference for them. Confidence comes instead from specification vectors frozen in 🧫️fixtures/🧭️detection-vectors.json and 🧫️fixtures/🗺️planning-vectors.json, each carrying the exact expected language and argv transcribed from the Go implementation this port reproduces, plus metamorphic laws asserted in the features (narrowing a scope never widens its plan; a filter only ever adds arguments; planning is idempotent).

Flattening and URI-path decoding are semio identifier rules with no external counterpart, but they are reachable today from two independently written implementations — the committed Go client and the new Rust crate — so this decision rests on those, cross-checked pairwise by the harness, plus the frozen selector vectors.
